audits.claim: Codex Dresdensis is dated by the holding institution to the later Postclassic, ca. 1300-1521; this is an institutional estimate, not a dated colophon.
audits.source_locator: SLUB 'The Maya Codex in the SLUB Dresden' page, bullet list (page has no folio or catalogue numbering)
audits.source_excerpt: originated in the later post-classical period of Maya culture (ca. 1300-1521) on the Yucatán peninsula
audits.basis: The holding institution's live page restates the range as its current account and presents it as an assessment with no colophon, calendar, or measurement citation, matching the entry's 'institutional estimate, not a dated colophon' framing. The same page states the codex 'consists of 39 sheets of bark bast', consistent with the screenfold description in §2.
audits.access_limit: The widely cited shelf mark Mscr.Dresd.R.310 does not appear on this page, so the entry's own flag on that shelf mark remains open; no object-level catalogue record was fetched.

audits.claim: Códice Maya de México (ex-Grolier) chain: allegedly cave-found in Chiapas, acquired by Josué Saenz around 1965, shown at the Grolier Club 1971, handed to Mexico 1974; the legacy radiocarbon range 1021-1154 circulates institutionally.
audits.entry_locator: source note [SLUB] (line 5); §2 table row 'Códice Maya de México (ex-Grolier)' (line 51); §8.2 (line 116)
audits.source_locator: SLUB 'Other Maya codices' page, section 'Mexico Codex'
audits.source_excerpt: acquired around 1965 by the economist and collector Josué Saenz, exhibited at the Grolier Club in New York in 1971 and handed over to the Mexican government in 1974
audits.basis: SLUB restates every element of the chain (cave find in the Chiapas highlands in the early 1960s; Saenz around 1965; Grolier Club 1971; Mexican government 1974) and prints the legacy radiocarbon figure 'written between 1021 and 1154 AD', with radiocarbon said to confirm the writing material (amate). INAH's own 2023 press page (audit meso-03) instead restates '1021 y 1152', so the legacy range varies across institutional retellings; this supports the entry's warning not to treat the announcement range as a timeless consensus.
audits.access_limit: SLUB gives no laboratory citation, sample details, or calibration data; the INAH/La Jornada 2018 announcement itself (jornada.com.mx) returned HTTP 403 and was not retrieved.

audits.claim: Códice Maya de México and Matrícula de Tributos are held by the Biblioteca Nacional de Antropología e Historia (BNAH, INAH), Mexico City.
audits.entry_locator: §2 table rows 'Códice Maya de México' and 'Nahua histories...' (lines 51, 54); source note [NCAT] (line 27)
audits.source_locator: INAH/Secretaría de Cultura press release, ENAH vault visit, paragraphs 5-6 and 8
audits.source_excerpt: documentos como el Códice Maya de México, dictaminado como el manuscrito legible más antiguo del continente americano
audits.basis: INAH states the Códice Maya de México and 'la Matrícula de Tributos, de filiación nahua' are among the treasures shown from the BNAH codex vault, and calls the Códice one of only four authenticated pre-Hispanic Maya manuscripts — corroborating both the BNAH custody claim and 'four Maya screenfolds survive' (§10). The same page dates its elaboration 'entre 1021 y 1152', the variant range noted in audit meso-02.
audits.access_limit: Press page, not a catalogue or shelf-mark record; gives no inventory numbers, and the 1152-vs-1154 variance is not reconciled by either institution page.

audits.claim: Paris codex: BnF, Manuscrits, mexicain 386; exact date unknown; BnF attributes a thirteenth-century copying hypothesis to Thompson rather than giving a secure date.
audits.source_locator: BnF Passerelles page, closing paragraph and 'Description technique / Provenance' block
audits.source_excerpt: On ne connaît pas la date exacte de ce document. Selon Thompson, archéologue spécialisé en études mayas, il s'agit d'une copie déformée d'un codex de l'époque classique (3e-9e siècle) réalisée au XIIIe siècle.
audits.basis: The BnF page states the exact date is unknown and attributes the thirteenth-century-copy hypothesis to Thompson, and its provenance block reads 'BnF, Manuscrits, mexicain 386' — matching the entry's attribution of a hypothesis rather than a secure date. SLUB's independent 'Other Maya codices' page offers a different non-secure estimate ('c. 1300 to 1500 AD'), consistent with the entry's discipline of keeping such dates source-attributed.
audits.access_limit: Passerelles is an educational presentation page; no palaeographic dossier or catalogue collation was inspected, and the entry's 'page-level readings are edition-specific' caution is untouched.

audits.claim: Popol Vuh: the extant text is transmitted through Ximénez's early-eighteenth-century manuscript, Ayer MS 1515, Newberry Library, Chicago; Ximénez claims to have transcribed the K'iche' text from indigenous sources.
audits.source_locator: University of Virginia Multepal reference page 'R.P.F. Francisco Ximénez', paragraphs 1-2
audits.source_excerpt: He is the author of the manuscript known as Ayer MS 1515, housed at the Newberry Library in Chicago... Ximénez compiled the work in 1701 and 1702 during his time as a parish priest in Santo Tomás Chichicastenango.
audits.basis: Coupling check (language + myth + era), not an isolated bibliography fact: the record ties the K'iche' text and its Spanish translation to a named physical witness (Ayer MS 1515, Newberry) and fixes the compilation to 1701-1702, i.e. the 'early-18th-c. manuscript' of the entry; it also states Ximénez 'claims to have transcribed the K'iche' text from various indigenous sources', matching the entry's transmission framing and its warning that composition dating and author identifications are reconstructions.
audits.access_limit: Project reference page; supplies no folio-level Newberry catalogue data and does not adjudicate authorship of the underlying K'iche' composition.

audits.claim: Rabinal Achí: living community performance tradition, proclaimed by UNESCO in 2005 and inscribed in 2008; recognition is of the performance tradition, not manuscript custody or proof of unchanged transmission.
audits.source_locator: UNESCO ICH element page 00144, status line and description paragraphs
audits.source_excerpt: Inscribed in 2008 (3.COM) on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity (originally proclaimed in 2005)
audits.basis: Coupling check (myth/performance/era): UNESCO's own record gives the 2005/2008 years and describes the drama as still performed on Saint Paul's day since colonization under cofradía coordination, with threats to its transmission — supporting 'living tradition under community custodianship' and the entry's warning that recognition does not prove unchanged transmission. The page says nothing about a Brasseur manuscript repository, so the entry's open gap stays open.
audits.access_limit: UNESCO nomination page describes the tradition, not manuscript custody; no repository check for the nineteenth-century written witness is possible from this page.

audits.claim: The Peabody Museum's Maya Corpus Program page describes active field and archival research begun in 1968 and offers published monument images from twenty sites plus an image-request form.
audits.source_locator: Peabody Museum 'Corpus of Maya Hieroglyphic Inscriptions' page, first paragraph
audits.source_excerpt: active field and archival research projects about ancient Maya inscriptions and art, begun in 1968... browse published images of monuments from twenty sites
audits.basis: The museum page confirms the 1968 start year, the twenty-site published image offering, and an image-request form, exactly as the entry summarises; the entry's own caution that this confirms an access point rather than a complete digitized archive is consistent with the page.
audits.access_limit: Page-level confirmation only; no image inventory or digitization coverage was checked, so the entry's 'not a complete digitized archive' limitation stands.

audits.claim: Motul dictionary tradition: the cited source lists Acuña's 1984 facsimile, Arzápalo Marín's 1995 edition, and Acuña's 2001 critical edition, but does not date the surviving manuscript copy (to-verify).
audits.entry_locator: source note [MOT] (line 34); §5 table row 'Motul dictionary tradition' (line 88)
audits.source_locator: Lehmann 'Colonial work on Yucatec Maya', Motul editions bibliography list
audits.source_excerpt: Ciudad Real, Antonio de 1984, Calepino maya de Motul. 2 vols. Edición de René Acuña.
audits.basis: The page lists the 1984 Acuña facsimile of 'the ms.', the 1995 Arzápalo Marín three-tome edition (vol. III paleographic transcription, vol. I heavily edited), and the 2001 Acuña critical and annotated edition — exactly the three-item edition chain in the entry — while citing 'the ms.' without any manuscript date. The flagged (to-verify) copy-date gap therefore remains genuinely unresolved and is not upgraded by this pass.
audits.access_limit: No manuscript-level dating on the cited page; the companion 'history' page was also fetched (Calepino placed in the early colonial record) and likewise gives no copy dates.

audits.claim: The Akademienunion project record for TWKM states a planned fifteen-year duration; a funding plan must not be converted into an observed completion date.
audits.source_locator: Akademienunion project database record I.B.17, project description
audits.source_excerpt: is funded with 5,42 Million Euros and is set to run for 15 years
audits.basis: The record confirms the fifteen-year plan, the Bonn location, and Nikolai Grube as project manager, and states no completion date — supporting the entry's caution and its 'harmonized end date is not established here' gap. A separate fetch of classicmayan.org confirmed the portal is live (title-level content only), supporting the access point.
audits.access_limit: No endpoint in the funding record; the Göttingen project schedule cited by the entry was not re-fetched, so the 2028/2029 divergence remains as recorded.

audits.claim: SN16: the ORA record supplies the peer-reviewed abstract, which describes recovered scenes and potentially unique genealogy under gesso — not a complete reading of the hidden Mixtec book.
audits.source_locator: Oxford Research Archive record, Abstract block
audits.source_excerpt: The results thus far indicate that the covered text contains unique genealogic information which may prove invaluable for the interpretation of archaeological remains from southern Mexico.
audits.basis: The retrieved abstract describes 'never before seen pictographic scenes hidden underneath a layer of gypsum and chalk gesso' and frames the genealogic information prospectively ('may prove'), i.e. as recovered scenes and a potential reading rather than a complete decipherment — matching the entry's phrasing for the Selden palimpsest. The record is marked peer-reviewed and deposits an accepted manuscript.
audits.access_limit: Abstract only; the article full text and the accepted manuscript file were not retrieved. The separate 'seven imaged pages' figure (attributed by the entry to a press release) was not re-fetched, so it remains press-release-level.

audits.claim: Memorial de Sololá: Penn, Ms. Coll. 700 Item 221, probably transcribed 1619-1650.
audits.entry_locator: source note [HIG] (line 30); §4 table row on Kaqchikel/highland annals (line 75)
audits.source_excerpt: Probably transcribed in Sololá, Guatemala, between 1619 (p. 15) and 1650 (Brinton).
audits.basis: Coupling check (Kaqchikel language + chronicle genre + copy era): the catalogue record gives the exact date range, the Penn Kislak Center call number, and language 'Cakchikel, with title page and marginal notes in Spanish', and lists Brasseur de Bourbourg and Brinton as former owners, aligning with the entry's copy-chain discipline. It also supports the entry's framing of these texts as colonial transcriptions of older matter rather than autographs.
audits.access_limit: Catalogue metadata page; the internal dated entries and the chronicle's content horizon were not collated against the entry's other claims.

audits.claim: The Florentine Codex is consultable through the Getty Research Institute's Digital Florentine Codex, an enhanced online edition with Nahuatl and Spanish transcriptions and translations.
audits.entry_locator: source note [FC] (line 9); §3 fol. 142r citation (line 61); §6 access layer (line 64)
audits.source_locator: Getty Research Institute 'Florentine Codex' project page, goal and outcomes sections
audits.source_excerpt: an enhanced online edition of the manuscript, complete with Nahuatl and Spanish transcriptions, English and Spanish translations, and searchable texts and images
audits.basis: The project page confirms an active digital critical edition of the Florentine Codex with Nahuatl and Spanish transcriptions (project active 2015-ongoing), supporting the entry's identification of a modern surrogate layer for [FC].
audits.access_limit: Folio-level queries (Book 12 fol. 19v; Book 10 fol. 142r) failed with network errors this pass, so the indexed folio citations and the digital-editor credit line recorded in the entry were not re-verified; nor was the manuscript's Laurenziana custody re-checked on a library page.

audits.claim: Solís et al. (2020) publisher abstract reports 991-1147 cal AD (ABA cleaning) versus 1159-1261 cal AD (Soxhlet plus ABA), with the authors preferring the latter; these are treatment-dependent support dates, not painting dates.
audits.entry_locator: source note [S18] (line 6); §2 table row 'Códice Maya de México' (line 51)
audits.basis: The publisher abstract could not be re-retrieved: Cambridge Core returned HTTP 429 on five attempts, including via the DOI link (doi.org/10.1017/RDC.2020.71). No independent copy of the abstract text was retrieved. The entry's recorded figures are therefore neither confirmed nor contradicted in this pass and must not be upgraded; the entry's own (to-verify) flags stand.
audits.access_limit: Cambridge Core rate limit prevented the abstract recheck; full text was already marked uninspected in the entry.

audits.claim: Madrid codex: the analytical study [MAD] places it in the Late Postclassic, probably the second half of the fifteenth century — a study estimate, not a secure colophon date.
audits.basis: The publisher page for Buti et al. (2014) returned HTTP 403 and no alternative full-text route was retrieved, so the entry's attributed dating could not be re-verified. An independent institutional page was retrieved instead (SLUB 'Other Maya codices'), which reports the Madrid codex as 'dated around 1500' and confirms the two-fragment acquisition history (Tro and Miró collections; joined by Léon de Rosny in 1881) — a nearby but not identical estimate, so the entry's source-attributed framing remains appropriate and no correction is warranted.
audits.access_limit: ScienceDirect 403; the citing source could not be read directly this pass.

audits.claim: Chilam Balam of Chumayel: Princeton record C0940 no. 4, 'between 1775 and 1800', acquired 1968; Roys (1933) introduction pp. 6-7 records a notation signed Juan Josef Hoil and dated 1782, which does not date every component of the compilation.
audits.entry_locator: source note [PUL] (line 8); §4 table row 'Books of Chilam Balam' (line 73)
audits.basis: Princeton DPUL met its bot-verification interstitial on three attempts ('Verifying connection... Verify You Are Human'), and the Roys 1933 introduction at sacred-texts.com returned HTTP 403; an archive.org guess for the printed volume returned HTTP 404. Neither the catalogue dating nor the 1782 Hoil notation could be re-verified, so the entry's record is preserved unchanged. The entry's own note that the live Princeton surrogate met bot verification is corroborated in kind.
audits.access_limit: Automated bot wall at dpul.princeton.edu and HTTP 403 at sacred-texts.com; no substitute full text retrieved.
